newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Proud, sad Black Watch lowers HK colonial curtain.
newsitem.headline: Proud, sad Black Watch lowers HK colonial curtain.

text.p: Kilted Scottish soldiers of the Black Watch regiment, last British unit to bid farewell to the Indian Empire 50 years ago, mounted a final guard in Hong Kong on Friday at an emotion-charged ceremony.

About 600 British supporters and a sprinkling of curious Chinese schoolchildren witnessed a bitter-sweet moment of colonial history four days before Britain returns Hong Kong to China after a century and a half of colonial rule.

The Black Watch arrived in Hong Kong in February as the final British battalion to serve before the June 30 handover, giving way to the People's Liberation Army of China. Soldiers guard military bases and perform flag ceremonies.

"We are sad but there is pride too. (The tune) 'Land of Hope and Glory' brings a lump to the throat," said British expatriate Rhona Chambers sheltering with other women onlookers under parasols in the sweltering heat.
Debonair composer-entertainer Noel Coward once sang in clipped tones of how "Only Mad Dogs and Englishmen go out in the midday sun."
But the soldiers of the Black Watch, resplendent in sporrans and kilts with 33 knife-edge pleats, had their own unique air-conditioning in the tropical humidity.

There were no embarrassing gusts of wind on the sun-baked parade ground and their commanding officer, Major Mike Onslow, confirmed: "The majority of the gentlemen are not wearing anything under their kilts."
At a flag-raising ceremony in April sniper Lance-Corporal Lee Wotherspoon was caught by a photographer as a gust of wind confirmed that there's nothing between a Scotsmen and his kilt.
He received romantic letters from women around the world admiring his clearly-visible "butt"-- and was reported only rebuked by his commanders because his socks were not level.

The regiment, which fought at Waterloo against Napoleon and Rommel at El Alamein, faced a delicate assignment in the dying days of empire here and Onslow did not envy the future job of China's new PLA garrison taking over from July 1.
"It is going to be so tricky for them as they are not the most sophisticated and cosmopolitan of people," he said.

Onslow was fiercely proud of troops who have fought in the Korean War and patrolled the backstreets of Belfast, the Northern Ireland capital. "My soldiers have done a great job in a very tricky situation," he said.
The last ceremonial mounting of the guard took place against a glorious backdrop encapsulating old and new Hong Kong.

Behind soared the gleaming skyscrapers of this capitalist goldmine, to the left stood the Convention Centre that will stage the handover to communist-ruled China . In front stood the frigate HMS Chatham, waiting to sail off into the sunset with the troops.
The final inspection complete, the troops marched off into history with a proud swagger in their step and a lone bagpiper playing his heart out.
Fresh-faced Watne Mackie, an 18-year-old private from Dundee, summed up the soldier's lament for all of them: "I am very, very sad to go. This is such a good place."
